# Career Preparation and Next Steps

##### The candidate who answered a question nobody asked

Two people interviewed for a data analyst role in Pune. Both were asked the same opening question: *"Walk me through a project you're proud of."*

The first described her methodology for eight minutes — the cleaning steps, the encoding choices, the hyperparameter grid, the cross-validation scheme. The interviewer's follow-up was "and what happened with it?" She had not deployed it and could not say who would have used it.

The second answered in ninety seconds: the business problem, the constraint that made it hard, what she built, the number it achieved against a baseline, and what she got wrong along the way. The remaining forty minutes were a conversation about her project, on ground she knew completely.

She got the offer.

The technical work was comparable. What differed was **framing** — knowing that an interviewer asks about a project to find out whether you understand why work matters, not to audit your grid search.

This final day turns forty-four days of skills into a job search, and the framing lesson runs through all of it.

##### The role landscape

"Data science" spans several distinct jobs, and applying to the wrong one wastes months.

| Role | Core work | Must-have skills | Entry difficulty |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Data Analyst** | Dashboards, SQL, business insight | SQL, Excel, Power BI/Tableau, communication | Most accessible |
| **Business Analyst** | Requirements, process, metrics | SQL, domain knowledge, stakeholder skills | Accessible |
| **Data Scientist** | Statistics, modelling, experiments | Python, statistics, ML, SQL | Moderate |
| **ML Engineer** | Productionising models | Python, software engineering, cloud, Docker | Harder |
| **Data Engineer** | Pipelines, warehouses, infrastructure | SQL, Python, Spark, cloud, orchestration | Moderate, undersupplied |
| **AI/GenAI Engineer** | LLM applications, RAG, agents | Python, APIs, prompt engineering, evaluation | Moderate, high demand |

Two honest observations about the Indian market.

**Data analyst is the most realistic first role** for most people entering the field, and it is a completely respectable route. Many strong data scientists spent two years writing SQL for a business team and learning a domain deeply — which is precisely the knowledge that makes later modelling work good.

**Data engineering is consistently undersupplied.** It attracts fewer applicants than data science, pays comparably, and the skills transfer well. If pipelines and systems interest you more than statistics, it is a shorter path with less competition.

Where the roles live: product companies and global capability centres in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Gurugram and Chennai; services firms everywhere; and a growing remote market. Product companies and GCCs generally pay substantially more, and the gap widens with experience.

##### The CV

One page for under five years of experience. It gets six seconds on the first pass.

**Lead with outcomes, not tools.**

```
Weak:   Used Python, Pandas and scikit-learn to build a classification
        model on customer data.

Strong: Built a churn prioritisation model (LightGBM) achieving 0.62
        precision@200 vs a 0.089 base rate, enabling an 11-person
        retention team to target the highest-value 200 calls per month.
        Deployed as a Streamlit app. [github.com/you/churn]
```

The structure that works for a career-changer or fresher:

```
NAME | City | phone | email | linkedin.com/in/you | github.com/you

SUMMARY (2 lines)
Data analyst with a supply-chain background, focused on forecasting and
operational analytics. Built and deployed three end-to-end projects
including a price forecasting tool now used by 40+ traders.

PROJECTS  ← put this FIRST if you lack experience
[3 projects, 2-3 lines each, each with a number and a link]

SKILLS
Python (Pandas, scikit-learn, LightGBM) · SQL (PostgreSQL, BigQuery) ·
Visualisation (Matplotlib, Plotly, Power BI) · Git · Streamlit · Docker

EXPERIENCE
[Even unrelated roles — reframe for transferable skills]
Supply Chain Analyst, [Company], 2022–2025
  · Reduced stockouts 18% by building a demand-tracking model in Excel/SQL
  · Automated a weekly report, saving 6 hours/week across the team

EDUCATION
[Degree, institution, year. Add relevant coursework if recent.]
```

**Projects before experience** if your experience is unrelated. The reader is deciding whether you can do the job, and your projects are the evidence.

**Reframe non-technical experience rather than hiding it.** Retail supervision becomes stakeholder management and operational metrics. Teaching becomes communication and explaining complexity. Domain experience in banking, healthcare or logistics is genuinely valuable, and candidates consistently undersell it.

Two practical notes: **quantify everything** you can (₹, %, hours, headcount, rows), and **tailor the summary line and skills order** per application. A generic CV performs measurably worse.

For LinkedIn: a keyword-rich headline (`Data Analyst | Python, SQL, Forecasting | Open to opportunities`), an About section written in first person that tells your transition story in three paragraphs, projects in the Featured section with images, and enough activity that your profile is not dormant. Recruiters search LinkedIn by keyword, so the words matter.

##### Technical interview preparation

Four rounds are typical. Prepare for all four, not just the one you enjoy.

**SQL** is the most-tested and most under-prepared skill. It appears in almost every data role interview.

```sql
-- The patterns that recur
-- 1. Top N per group (window functions)
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT city, product, SUM(revenue) AS rev,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY SUM(revenue) DESC) AS rn
  FROM sales GROUP BY city, product
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 3;

-- 2. Second highest (classic)
SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);

-- 3. Running total
SELECT date, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY date) AS running_total
FROM transactions;

-- 4. Month-over-month change
SELECT month, revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
             / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 0), 1) AS mom_pct
FROM monthly;

-- 5. Anti-join: who has no matching record?
SELECT c.* FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

-- 6. Self-join for consecutive days, retention cohorts, gaps
```

Practise on StrataScratch, DataLemur or LeetCode's database section. Twenty to thirty problems covering joins, window functions, CTEs and aggregation covers most of what is asked.

**Statistics and ML concepts.** Answer in a consistent shape: **mechanism, then trade-off, then a concrete experience.**

- Explain the bias-variance trade-off. When would you accept more bias?
- Why is accuracy misleading on imbalanced data? What would you use?
- What is p-hacking, and how does peeking at an A/B test cause it?
- How do you detect and prevent data leakage?
- Explain precision versus recall with a scenario where each matters more.
- Why does a Random Forest generalise better than a single tree?
- Central Limit Theorem — what it says and what it does not say.
- How would you handle missing data? What determines the choice?

A strong answer to the leakage question: *"Leakage is when information unavailable at prediction time reaches the model. The most common forms are fitting a scaler before the train/test split, feature selection outside cross-validation, and features recorded after the outcome. I prevent it with pipelines, and I check by looking for any feature correlating above 0.95 with the target. On my capstone I found exactly that — min and max price were recorded simultaneously with the target, and excluding them dropped my honest score from 0.61 to 0.79 on the corrected metric."*

Mechanism, trade-off, experience. The third clause only exists if you built something.

**The case round** presents a business scenario. The framework:

```
1. CLARIFY (2-3 min)   What decision? Who acts? What data exists?
                       What does success mean numerically?
2. STRUCTURE (2 min)   Lay out your approach before diving in
3. METRICS             Primary, secondary, guardrails
4. APPROACH            Baseline first, then escalate
5. TRADE-OFFS          Name what you are giving up and why
6. RISKS               What could go wrong; how you would know
```

The single biggest differentiator is **asking questions before answering**. Candidates who start designing immediately consistently score worse than those who spend three minutes on clarification.

**Behavioural** questions use STAR — Situation, Task, Action, Result. Prepare five stories in advance covering: a project you are proud of, a time you were wrong, a disagreement with a stakeholder, a time you had to explain something technical to a non-technical person, and a failure with what you learned.

The "time you were wrong" story is the one people fumble. Have a real one, tell it plainly, and say what changed in your process afterwards. Your capstone's "what I got wrong" section is already this story.

##### A realistic mock interview

Do this with a peer or an LLM, timed, out loud.

```
Round 1 — SQL (20 min)
  Given a schema of customers, orders and products:
  a) Total revenue per city for the last quarter
  b) Top 3 products by revenue in each city
  c) Customers who ordered in Jan but not Feb
  d) Month-over-month revenue growth per city

Round 2 — Concepts (20 min)
  a) Your model is 97% accurate. Should I be impressed? What do you need to know?
  b) Explain cross-validation and why a single split is insufficient.
  c) I have 500 rows and 300 features. What concerns you?

Round 3 — Case (25 min)
  "Our food delivery app has rising cancellations. How would you
   investigate, and what would you build?"

Round 4 — Behavioural (15 min)
  a) Tell me about a project you are proud of. (90 seconds, not 8 minutes)
  b) Tell me about a time you were wrong.
  c) How would you explain a confidence interval to a marketing manager?
```

Record yourself. Watching it back is uncomfortable and it is the fastest improvement available — you will notice filler, rambling, and the places where you answered a different question than the one asked.

##### The job search itself

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Target 10-15 specific roles, not 200 generic] --> B[Tailor CV per application]
    B --> C{Route in}
    C -->|Best| D[Referral: message someone at the company]
    C -->|Good| E[Direct application within 48h of posting]
    C -->|Weakest| F[Job board mass apply]
    D --> G[Screening call]
    E --> G
    F --> G
    G --> H[Technical rounds]
    H --> I[Case + behavioural]
    I --> J[Offer: negotiate]
    G -->|Rejected| K[Ask for feedback, log the gap, iterate]
    K --> A
```

**Referrals convert several times better than cold applications.** A short, specific message works:

> Hi [name], I saw your team's post about [specific thing]. I'm a data analyst who recently built [one-line project with result and link]. I noticed you're hiring for [role] — would you be open to a 15-minute chat about what the team works on?

Specific, brief, and gives them a reason to respond. Not "please refer me".

Apply within 48 hours of a posting where you can — application volume compounds fast, and early applications are read more carefully.

**Track everything** in a spreadsheet: company, role, date, route, contact, status, feedback. After twenty applications, the pattern in your rejections tells you what to fix. No callbacks means the CV or portfolio; failing technical rounds means SQL or concepts; failing case rounds means framing.

**Ask for feedback** after every rejection. Most will not respond; the ones who do give you the most valuable information in the whole process.

Set a realistic expectation: for a first data role in India, three to six months and fifty-plus applications is normal. Rejection volume is not a signal about you.

##### A continued learning plan

Choose a direction by year two. Generalists plateau; specialists compound.

| Path | Deepen | Signal you enjoy it |
|---|---|---|
| **Analytics/BI** | SQL depth, dbt, Power BI, experimentation | You like the business questions |
| **ML engineering** | Software engineering, Docker, cloud, MLOps | You like systems and deployment |
| **Data engineering** | Spark, Airflow, warehousing, streaming | You like pipelines and scale |
| **GenAI/LLM** | RAG, agents, evaluation, prompt engineering | You like the current frontier |
| **Domain specialist** | One industry, deeply | You like being the expert |

A three-month plan that actually works:

```markdown
## Next 3 months — Analytics Engineering

**Month 1**
- Advanced SQL: 30 window-function and CTE problems on StrataScratch
- dbt fundamentals course; build one small dbt project on public data
- Ship: a dbt project on GitHub with tests and documentation

**Month 2**
- Experimentation depth: Kohavi's book, chapters 1–8
- Rebuild the A/B testing framework from day 39 as a reusable package
- Ship: a blog post on the peeking problem with your own simulation

**Month 3**
- One cloud warehouse (BigQuery free tier)
- Contribute one merged PR to an open-source data tool
- Ship: a portfolio update with the new projects

**Weekly rhythm**
- Mon: 30 min reading (one paper or long-form article)
- Wed: 1 hour hands-on with the current focus
- Sat: 2 hours project work
- Monthly: publish something
```

Notice that every month has a **shipped artifact**. Learning that produces nothing visible is hard to sustain and impossible to demonstrate.

**Staying current without drowning:** timebox it, prefer depth over feeds, and filter by durability. SQL, statistics, experimentation and communication have compounded for decades. Most framework churn has not. You will miss things, and that is fine — fundamentals transfer, APIs do not.

##### Common mistakes

- Applying to two hundred roles with one generic CV.
- Leading with tools instead of outcomes.
- Preparing only for the ML round and being ambushed by SQL.
- An eight-minute answer to "tell me about a project".
- Designing immediately in a case round without clarifying.
- No "time I was wrong" story prepared.
- Hiding non-technical experience instead of reframing it.
- Never asking for feedback after a rejection.
- Waiting until you feel "ready" — you will not.
- Staying a generalist past year two.

##### Hands-on

Update your CV and LinkedIn to lead with outcomes and numbers, with projects positioned first if your experience is unrelated. Then run a full mock interview — one SQL question, one ML concept question, one behavioural question — timed and recorded. Watch it back and note three specific things to change. Repeat the same three questions two days later and compare.

For the mini-project, build a job-search kit: a tailored CV, an optimised LinkedIn summary, a list of ten to fifteen specific target roles at named companies with the reason each fits, a tracking spreadsheet, and a three-month learning plan for a chosen specialisation with a shipped artifact each month. Then take the first concrete action — send one referral message today. The kit without the action is procrastination with good documentation.

For the assignment, write out and answer five common interview questions mixing SQL, statistics, ML and behavioural, as if in a real interview. Write the answers in full, then read them aloud and time them. Anything over two minutes needs cutting; anything without a concrete example from your own work needs one adding.

##### Key takeaways

- Roles differ substantially — analyst is the most accessible entry point and data engineering is the most undersupplied.
- Lead with outcomes and numbers everywhere; the tools are visible in your repository.
- Answer technical questions as mechanism, then trade-off, then a concrete thing you built.
- Clarify before designing in case rounds, and prepare a real "time I was wrong" story.
- Track applications, ask for feedback, specialise by year two, and ship something every month.
